title: Q.Security Launches With $11.5M to Prepare Companies for Quantum Computing
excerpt: New York-based Q.security announced itself with a modest $11.5 million in seed funding, led by Castle Island Ventures with investment from New York Life Ventures and Coinbase Ventures.
content:
Q.security founders Guy Peer (r) and Nir Steinherz. (Courtesy: Q.security)

Quantum computing is not quite near. A broad consensus expects it to become real anywhere between 2030 and 2040. But that is no reason for enterprises to wait.

That is the view of New York-based Q.security, which just emerged from stealth, revealing a post-quantum cryptography (PQC) remediation platform that would address all the security risks hiding in enterprises. Q.security announced itself with a modest $11.5 million in seed funding, led by Castle Island Ventures with investment from New York Life Ventures and Coinbase Ventures. Other backers include Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund, a joint fund of SBI Holdings and Plug and Play, and Ground Up Ventures.

Q.security’s founders Guy Peer and Nir Steinherz come on the back of a success story in Unbound Security. That startup was co-founded by Peer, an alum of Israel’s Weizmann Institute of Science and former head of R&D at Sapiens, and Steinhertz, who served as head of strategy at Unbound. Unbound was acquired by Coinbase in 2022, after which Peer and Steinhertz spent four years working at the cryptocurrency platform before joining hands for this stealth startup.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Peer, who serves as Q.security’s CEO. “Nir and I founded Q.security to give enterprises the confidence to evolve the cryptography their business depends on. Our PQC remediation platform gives them lasting control over that evolution, so cryptography keeps pace with the business instead of holding it back.”

Q.security says its platform addresses enterprises’ needs from discovery to completion of their post-quantum remediation programs. For example, companies need business context to evaluate exposure, and decide which cryptographic findings to address first. Then there is also the question of how to use limited time and resources.

With its remediation platform mapping business structure and applications, Q.security promises cryptographic inventory in one coordinated remediation program. Also, its platform integrates with existing enterprise cybersecurity and infrastructure tools, and has a generous dose of AI built-in.

“Enterprises know they need to prepare for Q-Day, but understanding the associated risks is just the first step,” said Matt Walsh, general partner at Castle Island Ventures. With harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) data collection already under way, the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments, he added.

“Q.security…is providing security leaders with a practical path starting at assessment and ending in remediation. We believe the team’s deep expertise positions Q.security well to address one of the most significant emerging challenges in enterprise cybersecurity,” said Walsh.
